extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy, economic historians, and policy-minded readers
extracted.subtask_description: An 18th-century political-economy analysis of the causes of success and failure of joint-stock companies (especially in foreign trade), the effects of exclusive privileges (monopolies), and which kinds of trades are suitable for joint-stock organization. Includes historical examples and proposed governance reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managers' incentive misalignment (stewards of others' money)
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors and managers of joint-stock companies are often stewards of other people's money rather than their own, and therefore do not watch over it with the same anxious vigilance as private partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to negligence, profusion, and a tendency to consider attention to small matters as unnecessary; cited as a principal cause of mismanagement in many companies (general statement at start; examples include South Sea company failures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of exclusive privileges (monopolies) on company behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: An exclusive privilege tends to let companies mismanage and confine trade; monopolies do not reliably prevent folly or malversation among servants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While monopoly can shelter a company from competition, it often enables negligence and malversation (Royal African, South Sea, East India examples). A special-case justification exists (see 'temporary monopoly' criterion), but perpetual monopolies are criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint-stock companies rarely sustain open competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Without exclusive privileges, joint-stock companies for foreign trade have seldom been able to maintain competition against private adventurers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical record cited: Royal African and other companies failed when competing with private traders; private adventurers often outcompete joint-stock firms because of greater vigilance and adaptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size and dispersion of capital/ownership matters
rubrics_metrics.description: An immense capital divided among a very large number of proprietors tends to produce negligence and profusion; a joint-stock with moderate capital concentrated among few proprietors approaches a private copartnery and can achieve similar vigilance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hudson's Bay company offered as example of moderate capital and few proprietors leading to relative success; South Sea company contrasted as immense capital divided widely, encouraging mismanagement and stock-jobbing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trades suitable for joint-stock companies without monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: Only trades reducible to routine or uniform methods are practicable for joint-stock companies in open competition: banking; insurance (fire, sea risk, capture); building/maintaining navigable canals; supplying city water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These trades admit rules and predictable operations. Examples: bank of England and Edinburgh banks (banking), London Assurance and Royal Exchange Assurance (insurance), and navigable cuts/canals and water supply projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary monopoly as compensation for risky new trade
rubrics_metrics.description: A temporary monopoly may be justified when merchants undertake a new, dangerous, and expensive experiment in trade, as recompense for hazarding the experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogized to temporary monopoly granted to inventors or authors (patents/copyright). The monopoly ought to determine on expiration, forts/garrisons revert to government with payment of their value, and the trade be laid open to all subjects thereafter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance reforms to increase steadiness and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures such as raising voting qualifications, lengthening director terms with rotation, requiring a minimum holding period to vote, creating a governor-general and council for territorial administration, and establishing proper courts are proposed to make company governance steadier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These reforms (adopted after parliamentary inquiry into East India Company) were intended to increase dignity and steadiness of proprietors' and directors' courts but are noted as limited in remedying deeper incentive problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perils of agents' and servants' corruption and negligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Company factors, servants, and agents can engage in extortion, depredation, and profusion, causing large losses independent of external obstacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Royal African company factors, South Sea agents, East India servants acquiring fortunes or mismanaging revenues; anti-pattern: blaming foreign governments when internal malversation is often principal cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Companies with territorial rights are unfit to govern
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to possess forts and garrisons necessarily entails the right to make peace and war in those territories; joint-stock companies exercising such powers have frequently governed unjustly and capriciously and are unfit to govern great dominions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that states should take over territorial governance; East India Company's territorial acquisitions and subsequent inability to govern effectively are cited as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual monopolies tax the public in two ways
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpetual monopolies impose an absurd tax on the public by (1) raising prices (buyers pay more than under free trade) and (2) excluding subjects from profitable business opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxation benefits mainly to enable company servants to waste or embezzle surplus; defended as a general economic critique of monopolies' social cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint-stock companies are often more rule-bound than partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution of joint-stock companies makes them in general more tenacious of established rules than a private copartnery, and this can be an advantage in trades reducible to strict rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to suitability for banking and insurance where adherence to method reduces risk of speculative departures; departing from rules for speculation is dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical failure record as empirical criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The repeated historical failures of many joint-stock companies for foreign trade (even with exclusive privileges) serve as empirical evidence against the general suitability of the form for such trades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to Abbe Morellet's list of fifty-five failed companies since 1600 (with noted minor errors) and other historical examples like multiple African-trade companies, South Sea, and various East India difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition's long-run benefits (price reduction and production improvements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition may initially affect prices locally but in the long run lowers prices, encourages production, new divisions of labour, and improvements in art, thus benefiting consumers and production efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to rebut companies' complaints that competition 'ruined' markets; competition's dynamic effects are emphasized as desirable public outcomes.
